r41.argument: A partial reader might take 'I should be honest about what the swap cannot do' and the string of 'cannot' sentences as the writer doubting the swap's worth. But the paragraph is a deliberate concession, and ¶5 ('And yet. There is one thing the swap does...') and ¶6 ('a craft does not have to be large to be serious') show the writer remains confident in its value; the sentence's clause 'anyone who tells the school board otherwise is handing them an excuse' ties it directly to the funding stake the key names.
r41.stem_issue: The stem asks why the statement 'matters to the intended audience,' but the passage never identifies its audience or venue; only question 2 supplies the 'newsletter' framing. A test-taker must infer the audience from a sibling item or outside context rather than from the passage itself.

r41.argument: The boy 'stand[s] at the table for most of a lunch period deciding whether he could part with' the novel, which a reader might read as reluctance to be sympathized with. But the passage stresses the book 'is released because somebody decided another reader should have it' and that he 'seemed, if anything, pleased'; nothing says he was 'forced.' The key correctly identifies the anecdote's function of concretizing 'givers of books rather than only borrowers.'
r41.stem_issue: Stem labels the piece a 'newsletter' and its audience, information not present in the passage header or text; minor reliance on unstated context.

r41.argument: Option [2] closely paraphrases ¶2 ('The shelves did not empty overnight; they simply stopped growing... the gap between what they wanted to read and what they could find became a kind of quiet weather'), and a reader who weights the budget material heavily might take it as the thesis. But ¶2 is explicitly framed as 'The reason the swap exists,' i.e., background, while the 'less as a charity than as a craft' framing in ¶1 is picked up in ¶3 ('a craft is a thing you learn by doing it badly') and ¶6 ('a craft does not have to be large to be serious'), confirming the key.
r41.key_flaw: Justification cites 'sentence 4' and 'sentence 31' though the passage as presented is not sentence-numbered; the counts are accurate but the references are unusable by a reader of this version.

r41.argument: Option [0] correctly notes ¶5 uses 'a single narrative example' (the boy and the fantasy novel), but it misplaces the claim about giving in ¶4; that claim ('it makes children into givers of books rather than only borrowers') appears in ¶5 itself, while ¶4 is a list of what the swap 'cannot do.' No careful reader would choose it.

¶2's simile—'the way a town stops growing when the last factory closes and nobody notices until the graduating class is half its old size'—carries an implicit rebuke, and a reader might see the paragraph as criticizing the district. But the paragraph opens 'The reason the swap exists is not mysterious' and reports figures neutrally ('fell from roughly nine thousand dollars... to just over one thousand'); it never characterizes the district as careless, and ¶3 immediately pivots to 'what, exactly, does a book swap do,' supporting the key's reading.

'And yet.' does follow the concessions, so a hasty reader might call it a summary of them, but a two-word adversative fragment summarizes nothing; it introduces 'There is one thing the swap does that the library, even in its funded years, never quite did,' a pivot, not a recap. Nor is ¶5 the 'closing section'—¶6 follows.

r42.argument: The passage opens by promising to "honor that figure" and spends ¶1–2 and ¶6 on tribute: the mittens, "you waited for me in the snow," the page that "covered the share of dialysis the insurance would not, the gas... and three months of rent." ¶4 even insists "Nobody who gave did anything wrong; they did, in fact, something lovely." A reader who weights the frame paragraphs could call the purpose celebratory. But the writer explicitly pairs honoring with telling "the truth about it," and ¶3–5 ("Here is the part the eulogies have skipped"; "It does not work") make the argument dominant, so [3] captures only half the stated aim. Option [0] is contradicted outright by "Nobody who gave did anything wrong."

The passage does list "being photographed well" among the things that "deserving" has come to mean, and ¶2 lingers on the niece's photo ("grinning at someone out of frame"). A careless reader might tie the $1,100 figure to the photo. But the writer explicitly equalizes the template ("built with the same template") and resolves the contrast on "a man whom fewer people had met," so recognition, not the niece's skill, is the claim. [3] is directly contradicted by "same template."

"I want to honor that figure, and I want to tell the truth about it, and I am not sure the two can be done in the same breath" is the passage's announced thesis-like frame, and Q1's own key describes the purpose as both tribute and argument—so a reader could argue this sentence states the dual central concern better than a sentence covering only the critical half. However, it is a statement of intent and uncertainty, not a claim; the actual position the passage argues (that the system has "outsourced its stinginess") is the keyed sentence, which ¶5 then grounds and ¶6 restates ("something that should never have fallen to you at all").

¶4 does open by presenting the defenders' view ("I will concede what the defenders of these pages say"), so the first half of [0] is accurate. The second half fails: ¶5 introduces no new evidence about Aurelio; it offers a conceptual distinction ("between charity and justice") and refers to "the Aurelios of the world" generically. [3] is tempting because ¶5 literally says "It worked for her, for a while," but that is immediately negated ("It does not work") and ¶4 condemns the system, not the donors.

¶3 does contain some narrative detail—"a night-shift machinist," "His page, which his daughter built"—and the paragraph is explicitly offered as "the part the eulogies have skipped," which matches the sympathy angle of [3]. But the structure is a point-by-point match ("the same disease, the same clinic, and the same forty-mile drive... the same template") followed by the lone difference ("a man whom fewer people had met"), which is comparison, not narration. [2] invents a zero-sum causal claim the passage never makes.

A careless reader treating any semicolon as a 'pause' might pick [2], and the sentence does follow the concession "they did, in fact, something lovely." But nothing in the second clause softens anything: "it has outsourced its stinginess to the kindness of neighbors and then taken credit for the kindness" sharpens the accusation. [0] fails because the clause is the writer's own verdict, not the defenders' view; [1] fails because there is no list.

r43.argument: A reader might argue that by naming the exact figure ('140,000 dollars in savings') and diagnosing how the line item 'sits uneasily beside "algebra support" and "reading intervention"', the writers display fluency with the budget. But nothing claims superior expertise over the board; the sentences grant the board's reasoning ('We understand the logic') and its mandate ('nobody on this board was elected to protect dice') before the pivot 'But we would ask you to consider that the word "game" is doing some misleading work.' Option 3 has no real footing.
r43.key_flaw: Option 0 refers to 'the Guild,' an entity that never appears in the passage (the writers identify themselves only as 'the volunteers who have run the Thursday Design Lab'); this stray label makes the option non-parallel and signals it as a distractor by vocabulary alone. The justification's sentence counting is also loose: 'We understand the logic' is sentence 2 and the 140,000-dollar sentence is sentence 3, so the pair is sentences 2-3, but the explanation attributes the shortfall to 'sentences 2-3' collectively rather than to sentence 3.
r43.stem_issue: The stem's phrasing 'most likely matter to the board because they' is awkward and non-standard; it asks about the sentences' importance to the audience rather than their rhetorical function, which is what the options actually describe. A cleaner stem would be 'primarily function to.'

r43.argument: Paragraph 4 explicitly reuses Dario's story as the comparison for the budget: 'the document in front of you is itself a system of exactly this kind' and 'A budget, like Dario's village, is full of rules nobody wrote down.' So the anecdote does serve as evidence for the hidden-costs claim. However, paragraph 3 opens with 'Consider what happened...' immediately after paragraph 2's claim that 'Designing a game is different, because the designer must build the road, watch where it floods,' and it closes with 'No worksheet on ecology had ever gotten that far with him,' which ties it to the design-versus-reading/playing contrast. The 'primarily' qualifier favors the key; option 2 is a secondary, later application.
r43.key_flaw: The justification cites 'sentences 7-9' and 'sentences 12-16' without the passage being numbered, so the references cannot be verified by a test-taker; the substance is accurate.

r43.argument: The paragraph does enumerate costs ('in supervision hours, in a crowded homework room, or in the slower currency of disengagement') and its upshot is effectively that the projected savings are illusory: 'the district will pay for wherever that is.' A reader could map this onto 'the savings from cutting the Lab are overstated.' But these are not 'the district's spending categories' being listed—they are hypothetical displacement costs—and the paragraph's method is analogy ('a system of exactly this kind,' 'like Dario's village'), which option 0 captures precisely.
r43.key_flaw: The justification's sequencing is garbled: it says 'Sentences 18-20 call the budget... then sentence 19 enumerates,' placing sentence 19 after 18-20. Minor, but sloppy.

r43.argument: 'Slower currency of disengagement' does carry a quieter, more elegiac note than the preceding concrete items, and the paragraph ends with a pointed question ('Is it really more prudent to pull one piece out and hope the rest holds still?'), so one could call this a register shift. But the opening paragraph is not 'brisk'—it is measured and conciliatory ('We understand the logic')—and the phrase is clearly built on the sentence's financial frame: 'the district will pay for wherever that is, in supervision hours, in a crowded homework room, or in the slower currency.' The 'in... in... in' series makes disengagement one more item on the bill, which is exactly the key.

Because 'Some of them are.' directly contradicts the preceding 'nothing more ambitious than a card game about cats,' a hasty reader might see it as retracting the concession. But 'Some' is explicitly partial, and the very next sentence keeps the concession alive—'But the cat game, too, has an economy'—arguing that even the modest projects teach the lesson. So the concession is limited, not 'withdrawn entirely,' and nothing implies 'every Lab student' builds a complex system.

w41.argument: Option [2] keeps the price ('about 140 dollars') and frames it as an investment that 'would probably pay for itself many times over someday,' which is at least an attempt to speak to budget-minded members. But 'probably' and 'someday' are vague, and nothing in the passage shows how a free Wi-Fi booster would generate money for the garden. The key's comparison to 'last summer's new hoses' and the offer to 'pay half' concretely lowers the burden. Option [0] actually dismisses the concern ('honestly nothing'), and [3] drops the price entirely.

Option [0] fully delivers the explanatory half of the goal, and adds a concrete, verifiable detail ('the school stopped handing out printed packets two years ago') that the key lacks. However, it contains no acknowledgment of members who 'finished school without the internet,' so it fails the 'respects members' half of the two-part goal. The key's 'Many of you did homework with a library book and a pencil, but...' does both. Option [1] respects members but undercuts the argument ('the old way was always better'), and [2] is insulting.

Option [0] is a broad claim about 'students in rural areas across the country,' which a careless reader might take as a thesis, but it is a factual generalization, not an arguable position, and it previews none of the proposal (booster, table, vote). Option [3] merely restates sentence 5; [1] offers two sides without taking one. The key names both improvements and takes a position. Minor quibble: the key's 'safe place' introduces an idea (safety) the flyer never develops—the passage speaks of a 'cold car,' not danger—but this doesn't rescue any alternative.
w41.key_flaw: Key phrase 'a safe place' previews a safety rationale the flyer never develops; the passage's stated problem is a 'cold car' and weak signal, not safety.

w41.argument: 'For instance' would only work if the picnic table were an example of the booster, which it is not; sentence 10 describes a distinct improvement (table, outlet). 'In contrast' and 'As a result' misstate the relationship. No alternative has a real case; 'In addition' is plainly correct.

'Because of that concern, students using the table would agree to stay by the shed and to pick up before leaving each night' is grammatical and arguably logical: the concern is the reason the students would agree to the rules, so it does connect 13 to 12. However, it marks a cause-effect relation rather than explicitly labeling 13 as a 'response' to the worry, which is what the stem asks; 'To address that concern' does that directly. 'Despite' and 'Similarly' misread the relationship.

w42.argument: Option [2] does return to Arturo and implies the payoff of his second chance ("started his first semester of nursing classes at Ridgeline State University last fall and loves it"), which a reader might see as the strongest callback to the anecdote. But it contains no invitation to attend, so it satisfies only half of the stated two-part goal; the key alone does both ("Bring your transcripts on April 17" + "your own second start folded in your pocket" echoing sentence 7's "highlighted copy of that sheet folded into his jacket pocket").
w42.stem_issue: Stem says to replace sentence 12 only, so sentence 13 ("Hope to see you there.") remains; the key's invitation plus sentence 13 is slightly redundant, but not enough to undermine the item.

w42.argument: Option [0] is the only other choice that explicitly mentions parents ("many parents understandably dream of seeing their children attend one"), so a partial reader might choose it as 'addressing parents.' However, it concedes rather than addresses the belief that community college is lesser, and it offers no counterargument. The key speaks to "your teenager" and answers the concern directly with "the same degree at the end... smaller classes and far less debt." Option [2] fits sentence 9's returning-adult content but ignores parents entirely.

Option [2] ("one patron learned exactly which of his credits would transfer") does preview Arturo's story and gestures at transfer, so a reader might see it as previewing the post's movement. But it is a factual report, not a defensible claim, and it does not forecast the explanation of transfer pathways. The key makes an arguable claim ("clear transfer pathways can turn community college from a detour into a reliable second chance") and names both the anecdote ("As one patron's story shows") and the concept explained in paragraph 3.

Option [2] is a genuine analogy ("Earning a degree is like running a marathon"), so a reader scanning for 'analogy' might select it. But it explains the effort of earning a degree, not "what a transfer agreement guarantees," which the stem requires. The key's exchange-rate comparison directly clarifies the guarantee ("students know before enrolling what their coursework will be worth later") and sets up sentence 11's point about not losing credits.

Option [2] is concise and does define transfer pathways functionally ("deals that colleges make so your stuff from one school counts at the other one"), so a reader focused only on concision might pick it. However, "basically," "deals," and "your stuff" retain the casual register the stem asks to eliminate for a library blog. The key is equally concise and uses precise, professional diction ("formal agreements between colleges that guarantee credits earned at one school will count at another").

No alternative is defensible. [0] remains a comma splice (and adds a second one with "the sheet, it listed"); [3] uses "however" as a conjunctive adverb after only a comma, still a splice, and introduces a contrast absent from the original meaning; [1] "and so therefore" is redundant and imposes a causal relationship the original does not state. The semicolon in the key correctly joins the two independent clauses without altering meaning.

w43.argument: Option [1] is the only distractor drawn directly from the writer's observations ('the trumpets got softer... each time she did the hand thing'), so a reader focused on 'what her observations showed' might pick it. But it restates a single data point from paragraph 3 and ignores the breath evidence of paragraph 2 (sentences 5–6), so it does not 'sum up' how the conductor leads silently. The key [0] draws both strands together ('breath and hands'). Options [2] and [3] are a recommendation and an outside-knowledge generalization respectively, neither summarizing the observations.

Option [3] is an arguable claim and is grounded in the passage ('the musicians follow the conductor's breath more closely than her baton'), so it satisfies the 'claim requiring proof' half of the goal. However it previews only breath (paragraph 2) and omits the hand gestures of paragraph 3 ('She just lowered her left hand slowly, and the trumpets got softer'), so it fails the 'two kinds of silent signals' requirement. The key [0] names both and frames the paradox of leading silently. [1] is a definition, [2] is unprovable personal reaction.

Option [0] at least introduces the idea of control and sounds measured ('Some say... I agree'), but it endorses rather than qualifies the overstatement 'Conductors always control everything,' so it does not meet the 'qualifies' requirement. [1] intensifies the overstatement; [3] reverses it and contradicts the evidence that 'the trumpets got softer' when she lowered her hand. The key [2] limits the claim ('much of') and acknowledges she 'cannot play a note,' which fits sentence 3 ('makes no sound at all') and sets up the brass episode.

Option [3] is the only distractor that attempts to connect the two rehearsal moments to the breath-vs-baton claim, but it overreaches wildly ('proves,' 'baton is useless,' 'should stop using one'); the cellist only said players follow the breath 'more closely than her baton,' not that the baton is useless. [1] and [2] are irrelevant background. The key [0] correctly reads the together/ragged contrast (sentences 5–6) as evidence that players time their entrance to her breath.

Option [0] is concise and retains the 'each time' idea, but the relative clause 'which happened each time' is misplaced between subject and verb, obscuring what happened each time and breaking the cause-effect clarity the stem demands. [1] uses 'although,' which wrongly signals contrast rather than cause-effect. [3] is a comma splice with a passive opening that hides the agent. The key [2] 'Each time she slowly lowered her left hand, the trumpets softened' is concise and makes the repeated causation explicit; dropping 'pretty awesome to see' is consistent with the concision goal.

w44.argument: Option [0] is the only other choice that explicitly mentions college ("whatever college pool I find next fall") and ties it to her Harrow Street experience, so a reader focused on the surface requirement 'connect pool to college' might pick it. But it describes her as a swimmer, not as a 'member' of a community; it ignores the essay's actual lesson in sentence 12 about showing up and speaking up for shared spaces. Option [2] echoes both strands of the essay ("knows the regulars by name" recalls Mr. Okafor; "shows up at the meeting" recalls the budget hearing).

Option [0] continues the anecdote in sentence 6 ("The girl practiced floating every afternoon after that") and so feels like a natural follow-on, but it documents the girl's swimming progress, not a connection between people who 'would never otherwise meet.' Option [3] explicitly establishes they were strangers ("Neither knew the other's name") and that the relationship persisted across households ("her mother was bringing him tomatoes"), directly evidencing sentence 5.

Option [2] softens 'Everyone' to 'Nearly everyone,' which a careless reader might take as acknowledging dissent, and it preserves her position. But it never states what the differing view was or who held it, so it does not 'acknowledge that some residents held a different view' in any substantive way. Option [0] names the dissenters' concern ("worried about rising taxes... repairing roads") while keeping 'Many residents opposed the idea' as the main clause.

Option [1] is formal and clearly conveys strong frustration ("unconscionable betrayal"), so a reader equating 'appropriate tone' with elevated diction might choose it. However, its melodrama ("a wound upon the very soul of Calder Falls") is as immature as the slang it replaces. Option [0] is measured and supplies the concrete reason (echoing sentence 10's working parents). Option [3] is appropriately formal but conveys no frustration at all.

Option [1] keeps the original's 'show up and speak up' pairing, which the key drops, so one could argue it preserves slightly more of the original wording. But it retains the very redundancy the revision targets ("What I learned is that I learned that") and omits the 'where the decisions... get made' clause, so it fails on both concision and meaning. The key's omission of 'willing to show up' is minor since 'speak up for it where decisions are made' entails showing up.
w44.key_flaw: The justification claims the key keeps 'the full idea,' but the key drops the original's 'willing to show up' element; the loss is slight and arguably implied by 'where decisions are made,' but the justification overstates completeness.

w45.argument: Option [3] does literally 'address this worry directly' — it names the inexperienced reader ('Anyone who has never held a shovel') and tells them 'they are still welcome to come along.' A reader focused only on the stem's words 'addresses this worry directly' might pick it. But the stem frames the writer's purpose as overcoming hesitation, and [3] reinforces the fear ('will probably slow the crew down'), so it undercuts the goal that [1] serves with reassurance and a concrete training detail. Options [0] and [2] do not touch the worry at all.
w45.stem_issue: The stem could be slightly tighter: 'addresses this worry' does not by itself say 'reassures,' though the context (hesitation to volunteer, a recruiting paragraph) makes the intended goal clear.

w45.argument: Option [3] is the only other choice that links volunteer shortage to trail damage ('a trail without enough volunteers will eventually fall apart'), so a partial reader might see it as supporting the point. However, it is a generalization about the future ('eventually'), not evidence that last year's shortfall 'actually harmed the trail,' and 'Everyone knows' is an unsupported appeal. [0] describes success, not harm; [1] is about hiker numbers. The key [2] gives a specific, dated consequence ('stayed blocked by fallen trees until the middle of August') that follows the 'thirty-one showed up' sentence logically with 'As a result.'

Option [1] is the only other choice that is grammatically a comparison ('even longer than the Tamsett, some stretching hundreds of miles'), so a reader skimming for 'comparison' might select it. But it compares trail lengths, not the forty feet in sentence 7, and it does not help readers 'picture how little forty feet is.' [0] is a definition of a pulaski; [2] is a personal anecdote about path smoothness. The key [3] ties forty feet to 'the hallway outside our cafeteria, a walk that takes most of us ten seconds,' a familiar school reference that fits the classmate audience.

Option [0] is respectful and avoids the insult in sentence 12 ('you're kind of being lazy'), so a reader prioritizing 'respectful' might accept it. But its bureaucratic register ('is hereby recommended to all members of the student body') is neither encouraging nor suited to an appeal to classmates, and it barely 'urges.' [1] keeps the insulting tone ('care more about their phones'); [2] is so permissive ('totally fine if you would rather sleep in') that it fails to urge at all. The key [3] uses inclusive 'us'/'our' and a motivating claim ('a single Saturday of our work can make a real difference'), matching the stated tone.
